title: Sandur: Building a Connected Subsea Cable Inspection Demonstrator
author: Paris Mollo
summary: A workbench demonstrator that connects sensing, motion, embedded software, mechanical design, and cloud connectivity to explore subsea cable inspection.

content.text: Hi, I'm Paris Mollo, and this is my first blog post. I hope you enjoy reading it.

Subsea cables are easy to forget because we rarely see them. [Yet they form the physical backbone of intercontinental internet connectivity](https://www.submarinecablemap.com/). Despite lying beneath the sea, these cables remain vulnerable to damage: fishing vessels and dragged anchors cause most cable faults, while earthquakes and other environmental events also contribute. [TeleGeography's Submarine Cable FAQ](https://www2.telegeography.com/submarine-cable-faqs-frequently-asked-questions) provides a clear overview of how these cables work, where they are installed, and why they sometimes fail.

content.highlight: It is to verify that the cable remains protected
content.text: The challenge is not only to confirm that a cable was buried correctly when it was installed. It is to verify that the cable remains protected months and years later.

content.highlight: It is not an underwater vehicle and does not attempt to reproduce real marine conditions.
content.text: To explore this problem, I spent part of this summer building a small connected demonstrator as a personal project. It is not an underwater vehicle and does not attempt to reproduce real marine conditions. Instead, it models the core inspection loop: (1) move a sensor along a route, (2) collect measurements at known positions, (3) and send the resulting data to a remote system. The demonstrator combines sensing, motion, embedded software, mechanical design, and cloud connectivity.
This article explains how I designed the demonstrator, how each part works, and how the pieces fit together.

content.title: Project disclaimer
content.text: Sandur is a personal project I built for learning and fun. It is a simple concept demonstrator, not a real production-ready solution, and it probably has hundreds of flaws.
1. The idea

content.highlight: which means that a safely buried section can gradually become exposed.
content.text: A subsea cable can stretch for hundreds or thousands of kilometres. Installing it below the seabed helps protect it, but as we all know, the seabed is not static. Sediment shifts and sand cover changes, which means that a safely buried section can gradually become exposed.

Traditional inspections require specialised vessels and underwater vehicles. These systems are essential, but they are also expensive to deploy and are often used reactively or at scheduled intervals. This makes frequent inspection difficult.

For this personal project, I imagined a different model: many smaller autonomous systems, each responsible for a limited section of cable and able to report what it observes. I wanted to explore the idea and enjoy the engineering process, not design something ready for real-world deployment.
The full idea uses two types of vehicle:

items: An autonomous underwater vehicle that travels along the cable and records measurements.
A surface vehicle that acts as its docking station, communications relay, and connection to the internet.

content.text: [Radio signals do not travel well through seawater](https://www.hydro-international.com/article/underwater-electromagnetic-propagation), so the underwater vehicle cannot depend on a continuous cloud connection. It must complete its mission locally, store its observations, and transfer them after returning to the surface station.

content.highlight: I reduced the idea to five essential functions:
content.text: I could not build that entire system in one summer. Instead, I reduced the idea to five essential functions:

items: Move a sensor along a known route.
Measure the surface below it at regular positions.
Combine each measurement with its position.
Send the resulting inspection records to a remote system.
Preserve the latest machine state so it can be observed and configured remotely.

content.text: That simplified model became Sandur. It may not be as ambitious as the original concept, but it was a practical place to start.
2. The concept

Sandur is a rail-mounted inspection demonstrator. A small carriage moves along an aluminium rail above a model surface. A distance sensor on the carriage looks down and measures the shape below it. A PVC pipe represents the cable.

content.alt: Hand-drawn Sandur concept diagram showing the sensor carriage on an aluminium rail, the motor and gateway node, a buried pipe, the six-step inspection cycle, and the resulting cloud inspection map.
content.caption: Figure 3. The Sandur concept: a rail-mounted sensor, its inspection cycle, and the data flow to the cloud.

content.highlight: instead models the information flow: move, observe, associate the observation with a location, and transmit the result.
content.text: The demonstrator is not trying to reproduce underwater sensing physics. A real inspection system could use a sub-bottom profiler or another instrument capable of detecting structures beneath sediment. Sandur instead models the information flow: move, observe, associate the observation with a location, and transmit the result.
The system is split into two embedded nodes:

items: **The sensor node** travels on the carriage. It reads a grid of distance measurements and sends them wirelessly.

**The motor and gateway node** stays at the end of the rail. It moves the carriage, requests measurements, combines each sensor frame with the carriage position, and publishes the result through the internet.

content.highlight: but that would introduce drag, snagging, and cable-management problems
content.text: I split the work this way for a practical reason. I could run a data cable to the moving carriage, but that would introduce drag, snagging, and cable-management problems. A wireless link keeps the moving assembly simpler, while the fixed node handles the motor wiring, Wi-Fi connection, and secure cloud connection.
An inspection cycle works as follows:

items: The carriage returns to its manually defined zero position if necessary.
It moves towards the endpoint in configured intervals, shortening the final interval when needed.
It stops and measures the surface below.
The measurement is associated with its position along the route.
The resulting inspection record is sent to a remote system.
This process repeats until the carriage reaches the endpoint, after which it returns to the start.

content.text: A full run therefore produces a sequence of 8 × 8 distance frames, each associated with a position along the rail.
3. How I built it
3.1 Electronics

The electronics are organised around two ESP32 development boards. [An ESP32 is a small microcontroller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESP32) with enough processing power for sensors and motor control, plus built-in Wi-Fi and short-range wireless communication.
Using two controllers gave each one a clear responsibility.
Sensor node
The moving node contains:

items: One ESP32 development board
One VL53L5CX time-of-flight sensor
A 5 V USB power source

items.alt: Pinout diagram of an ESP-WROOM-32 development board showing its GPIO, power, communication, touch, ADC, and DAC pins.
items.caption: Figure 4. ESP32 development-board pinout and available interfaces.

items.alt: VL53L5CX time-of-flight distance-sensor carrier board with its optical sensor, regulator, passive components, and connection pads visible.
items.caption: Figure 5. The VL53L5CX 8 × 8-zone time-of-flight distance-sensor carrier used by the moving node.

content.text: A [time-of-flight sensor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time-of-flight_camera) measures distance by emitting light and measuring how long it takes for the reflection to return. Since light travels at a known speed, the return time can be converted into distance.

content.highlight: This matters because a single measurement only says how far away one point is. A grid begins to describe shape.
content.text: The VL53L5CX does not return only one distance. It divides its field of view into an 8 by 8 grid, producing 64 measurements per frame. This matters because a single measurement only says how far away one point is. A grid begins to describe shape. If part of the surface is raised, lowered, or interrupted, neighbouring zones can reveal that change.

content.highlight: The firmware uses this status to distinguish valid distances from weak or unusable measurements.
content.text: Each zone also has a status value. The firmware uses this status to distinguish valid distances from weak or unusable measurements. Treating every number as trustworthy would create false structure in the resulting surface map.
Motor and gateway node
The fixed node contains:

items: One ESP32 development board
One NEMA 17 stepper motor
One DRV8825 stepper motor driver
A 12 V motor power supply
A separate 5 V USB supply for the ESP32

items.alt: NEMA 17 stepper motor with a square metal faceplate, protruding shaft, black motor body, and four coloured wires.
items.caption: Figure 6. The NEMA 17 stepper motor that drives the carriage along the rail.

items.alt: DRV8825 stepper motor driver carrier board with a purple circuit board, adjustment potentiometer, driver chip, and connection pins.
items.caption: Figure 7. The DRV8825 carrier that translates ESP32 control signals into stepper-motor current.

content.highlight: The ESP32 tells the driver which direction to move and sends one pulse for each motor step.
content.text: A microcontroller cannot power a stepper motor directly. Its pins produce logic signals, not the voltage and current required by motor coils. That's why we have the DRV8825 between the controller and the motor. The ESP32 tells the driver which direction to move and sends one pulse for each motor step.

content.highlight: This provides a simple position model without adding a separate position encoder.
content.text: A stepper motor is useful here because motion is divided into discrete steps. If the controller has sent 200 forward steps and no steps were missed, it can treat the carriage as being 200 steps from its starting point. This provides a simple position model without adding a separate position encoder.

content.highlight: In this version, I place the carriage at the start and define zero manually before an inspection
content.text: That simplicity has a limitation: step count is an estimate, not physical proof. If the motor stalls or the belt slips, the software position and real position can diverge. In this version, I place the carriage at the start and define zero manually before an inspection. Future versions could add limit switches or an encoder for automatic homing and position verification.
3.2 Sensor connections
The distance sensor connects to the moving ESP32 through [I2C](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I2C), a short-distance digital bus that uses two signal wires:

items: **SDA** carries data.
**SCL** carries the clock that coordinates each transfer.

content.text: The firmware configures the sensor for an 8 by 8 grid and reads frames at 10 Hz. This provides a new surface map roughly every tenth of a second, although the gateway only records a frame when the carriage reaches an inspection point.
Wireless link between the boards
The two ESP32 boards communicate using [ESP-NOW](https://www.espressif.com/en/solutions/low-power-solutions/esp-now). This is a direct, low-overhead wireless protocol between nearby ESP32 devices.
The gateway sends a small capture request containing a sequence number. The sensor node replies with:

items: The same sequence number
64 distance values
64 measurement-status values

content.text: 3.3 Firmware
Sandur has separate firmware for the sensor node and the motor/gateway node.
Sensor firmware

On the sensor node, I continuously sample distance frames and keep the latest complete one. I only send that frame when the gateway requests a capture, so sensor sampling stays independent from inspection timing.
Motor control firmware
Motor movement is non-blocking, so the gateway can process serial commands, wireless packets, MQTT traffic, and state updates between motor steps.

I use a state machine to coordinate movement, captures, and the return to zero. At each measurement stop, the gateway requests a frame and waits up to one second. If none arrives, it records an error and continues. For valid replies, it stores the mission identifier, capture sequence, motor position, 64 distance measurements, and their validity statuses.
Local control
A USB connection lets me control the carriage locally. From the browser panel, I can move it, set its limits, start or stop an inspection, and check its current state.
3.4 Cloud application with IoT Core

I connect the fixed gateway to IoT Core, which acts as the secure entry point between the physical demonstrator and the cloud. The gateway communicates using [MQTT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MQTT), a lightweight messaging protocol commonly used by connected devices, over an encrypted mutual TLS (mTLS) connection.
The gateway has its own digital certificate, which allows IoT Core to verify the device's identity. A narrowly scoped policy then controls what the device is allowed to send and receive.

After each measurement, the gateway publishes an inspection record with the sensor data and its position along the rail. An IoT rule then archives the record in Amazon S3, so I can review the history of the inspection run later.

I also use a Device Shadow, a persistent cloud document that stores the latest known state of the demonstrator. It lets a remote application see information such as the carriage position and movement state, and request a limited configuration change even when the device is temporarily disconnected.

content.highlight: If the network goes down, the carriage can keep moving and measuring locally
content.text: The inspection itself does not need a cloud connection. If the network goes down, the carriage can keep moving and measuring locally. The gateway tries to reconnect in the background and resumes cloud communication once the connection returns.
3.5 Mechanics: rail, enclosures, and 3D printing

The carriage moves along a V-slot aluminium rail. A stepper motor pulls it using a GT2 timing belt stretched between a motor pulley and an idler, converting the motor's rotation into straight, controlled movement.
I designed and 3D-printed custom parts to mount the rail inside a wooden box that I built from 15 mm plywood. These include the motor mount, end supports, sensor enclosure and controller enclosure.

content.text: 4. Demo

Once I had the rail assembly working, I went to a wood shop here in Paris and ordered some plywood panels. I put the wooden box together in probably the worst possible way, but it was good enough to test the idea.
I screwed the rail supports into the box and then installed the rest of the components.

Then I built a small UI to visualise the data in the browser, which made it easier to demonstrate the idea of scanning the seabed surface. I also added a pipe to represent the cable and a threshold showing the minimum sand cover. If the measured surface drops below that threshold, the cable would be considered exposed.

content.text: 5. Final considerations
Since I built this in my spare time and it was never really a priority, the project still has a good bunch of issues. Let me list a few of them, haha:

items: The support brackets on both sides of the aluminium rail are not ideal for quickly mounting and removing it, especially with a fixed-length box.
The ToF sensor has a limited field of view, roughly 63° diagonally.
The system is noisy.
The wiring and cable management are terrible in this version. It works, but it is definitely not pretty.

The VL53L5CX is not designed for underwater inspection, and its optical measurements would be strongly affected by water clarity, scattering, range, and packaging. A real buried-cable inspection system would likely require an acoustic instrument such as a sub-bottom profiler, or another purpose-built sensing technology.
The current visualisation combines the measurements into a simplified surface model. It is useful for explaining the concept, but it is not yet a calibrated or precise reconstruction.

content.text: I hope you liked the article. It was my first one, so I'm still figuring out which parts of the process are interesting to share and which are not. If you have any feedback, feel free to reach out by email or find me on LinkedIn and GitHub.
